newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurocourt rules against Turkey on Cyprus case.
newsitem.headline: Eurocourt rules against Turkey on Cyprus case.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights, in a landmark judgment, ruled on Wednesday that Turkey had violated the rights of a Greek Cypriot who lost her land in northern Cyprus when Turkish troops invaded in 1974.

In a widely-watched case, the Court dismissed Turkey's argument that the European human rights convention did not apply to its occupation of the north of the Mediterranean island since it had occurred before Ankara accepted its jurisdiction.

The court also rejected Turkey's contention that expropriation was legal under the constitution of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, an entity recognised only by Ankara, declaring that the Turkish army "exercised effective overall control there".
By 11 votes to six, the Court ruled that Turkey had violated tourist guide Titina Loizidou's property rights by denying her access to plots of land she owned in Kyrenia, northern Cyprus.

When she tried to return there in March 1989 with a Greek Cypriot group called "Women Walk Home", she was arrested by Turkish Cypriot police in Nicosia and returned via United Nations officials to the Greek Cypriot sector.

The Court, an arm of the 40-nation Council of Europe which promotes democracy and human rights, gave Turkey six months to submit observations on Loizidou's claim for "just satisfaction", reserving its judgment on that point.

"I am very satisfied," Loizidou told reporters. "This is a historic decision: It is the first time an international court has taken a legal decision on Turkey's responsibility in northern Cyprus and found Turkey guilty for denying people the right to enjoy their property."

However, the Court dismissed her claim that she had lost her home, noting that she had not been living in Kyrenia at the time and that her intention to live in one of the flats she had been building in northern Cyprus did not constitute residence.

A significant part of the ruling was the rejection of Turkey's claims that the case was outside the Court's purview, partly because it related to events before 1990, when Ankara accepted the compulsory jurisdiction of the Strasbourg court, and partly because it was outside Turkish territory.
Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 in response to a coup engineered by the then military junta in Greece.

"The Court observed that the concept of 'jurisdiction' under the (European Convention on Human Rights) was not restricted to national territory. In particular, the responsibility of a contracting state could arise when it exercised effective control in an area outside its national territory as a result of military action," a Council of Europe statement said.

"In the Court's view, it was obvious from the large number of troops engaged in active duties in northern Cyprus that the Turkish army exercised effective overall control there. In the circumstances of the case, this entailed Turkey's responsibility for the policies and actions of the 'TRNC'," it said.
